exam: A 28‑year‑old farmer presents after a fall on an outstretched hand with a swollen, painful wrist. What is your immediate management? — Assess distal pulses, obtain a wrist X‑ray, immobilise in a splint if fracture suspected.

A patient with known sickle cell disease has sudden hand pain, swelling and fever. How do you differentiate vaso‑occlusive crisis from septic arthritis? — Examine for joint effusion, obtain joint aspiration; vaso‑occlusive pain is diffuse, aspiration yields sterile fluid.

During a routine exam you note weakness of wrist extension but normal sensation. Which nerve is likely involved and what injury mechanism is common? — Radial nerve; often injured in humeral shaft fractures or compression from a tight cast.

A child presents with a swollen elbow, limited motion and a fever of 38.5 °C. What investigations are essential and why? — Plain X‑ray to rule out fracture, joint aspiration to detect septic arthritis; both guide urgent treatment.

In a resource‑limited clinic you suspect TB osteomyelitis of the humerus. Which clinical clues support this and what is the treatment principle? — Chronic pain, low‑grade fever, weight loss; start anti‑TB therapy for 6‑9 months after confirming with biopsy if possible.

A patient on antiretroviral therapy develops a painful, tender forearm swelling after a minor injury. What complication must you rule out and how? — Compartment syndrome; assess pain on passive stretch and consider urgent fasciotomy if pressure high.

Why is NSAID use cautioned in a patient with a known peptic ulcer presenting with shoulder bursitis? — NSAIDs increase gastric bleeding risk; consider paracetamol or intra‑articular steroid injection instead.

A manual worker complains of gradual shoulder pain worsened by overhead activity. What is the most likely diagnosis and first‑line management? — Rotator cuff tendinopathy; advise activity modification, physiotherapy and NSAIDs if no ulcer risk.
ai.title: Upper Limb Assessment
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: The upper limb includes the shoulder, arm, elbow, forearm, wrist and hand. Understanding anatomy, common injuries and infections helps clinicians diagnose and manage problems efficiently, especially where resources are limited.

b: Shoulder: glenohumeral joint, rotator cuff, suprascapular nerve
Wrist/hand: complex carpometacarpal joints, digital nerves
sections.p: The upper limb is a functional unit that moves the hand for tasks. It is supplied by the brachial plexus, major vessels (subclavian, axillary, brachial) and muscles that cross each joint.

b: Pain localisation → joint vs. soft‑tissue vs. nerve
Red flag symptoms → vascular compromise, infection, compartment syndrome
Common tropical contributors: HIV‑related neuropathy, TB osteomyelitis, malaria‑related myalgia
sections.p: Clinicians must link history (trauma, infection, systemic disease) to localisation of pain, weakness or swelling, then use a focused exam to narrow differential diagnoses.

b: Compartment syndrome: pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch, tense swelling
Septic arthritis: acute mono‑articular pain, fever, limited active motion
Peripheral neuropathy: sensory loss in a nerve distribution, often HIV‑related
sections.p: Upper‑limb problems are frequent in low‑resource settings due to road traffic injuries, manual labour, and infections. Early recognition of compartment syndrome, septic arthritis and neurovascular injury can prevent permanent disability.

t.b: Does the bone show fracture or dislocation? → Guides immobilisation or surgery; if unavailable, rely on clinical alignment and neurovascular exam
Is the joint fluid purulent? → Confirms septic arthritis; if unavailable, treat empirically if clinical picture fits
Is there demyelination or axonal loss? → Helps differentiate compressive vs. systemic neuropathy

b: Palpate bony landmarks and tender points
Active and passive range of motion at each joint
Strength testing of deltoid, biceps, triceps, wrist extensors/flexors, hand grip
Sensory testing in median, ulnar and radial distributions
sections.p: Examination proceeds from proximal to distal, assessing skin, bones, joints, muscles and nerves. Compare both sides.

b: Missing a pulse deficit in a supracondylar fracture
Treating presumed tendonitis without ruling out fracture
Relying on normal white cell count to exclude infection in immunocompromised patients
sections.p: Errors often arise from incomplete localisation, overlooking vascular status, or assuming infection without joint aspiration.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly expanding swelling with pain on passive stretch (compartment syndrome)
Fever with joint swelling and limited motion (suspected septic arthritis)
